notes.meaning: Paul calls them "brothers," so he sees them as real believers. But they acted "worldly." That means they were led by selfish human desires more than by God's Spirit. They had new life in Christ, but it was weak, like a baby's.

"Milk" means the first and plainest truths of the gospel. "Solid food" means deeper teaching. It is the same gospel, just taught in a way they could take in. Paul does not blame them for starting as babies. He blames them for not growing up.

Paul gives proof that they are still worldly. There is jealousy in their hearts, quarrels in their words, and splits in their actions. "Walking in the way of man" means living just like people who do not know God. Paul is describing how they behave, not saying they are unsaved.

Picking favourite preachers shows the problem plainly. Paul even scolds the people who were his own fans, so no one could think he wanted praise. Paul and Apollos taught the same message. Taking sides over them was about outward style, not truth.

Paul asks bluntly what he and Apollos really are. They are servants, and the people believed through them, not in them. God gave each one his job and his gifts. So it makes no sense to name parties after them.

Paul started the church in Corinth, and Apollos came later and kept teaching them (Acts 18). They are like a farmer who plants and one who waters. Only God can make the seed grow, and he kept doing that through both men.
Next to God, the workers are nothing worth boasting about. Their work still matters, and God normally uses it. But the growth, and so the glory, belongs to God alone.

The planter and the waterer are on one team with one goal: saving people. So they should never be turned into rival leaders. Each will be rewarded by God for his own faithful work, not for how much success he had.

The workers serve under God, with him and for him. The church does not belong to Paul or Apollos. It is God's field and God's building. Paul now switches from the farming picture to a building picture.

Paul says he was a skilled builder, but only because God's grace made him one. He laid the foundation when he started the church. Others build on it later. Each of them must take great care that what he adds fits the foundation.

Jesus Christ himself is the only foundation, and he is already laid. No other can be put in his place. A church not built on him is not a true church. Even so, people can still build badly on the right foundation.

Some build with materials that last, like gold, silver and fine stone. Others use wood, hay and straw, which burn. This mainly means what teachers teach and build into the church. It may be sound truth, or empty human ideas that do not last. "The Day" is the day the Lord returns to judge, and the fire is a picture of his test. It shows what kind of work each person did, not just how much.
If someone's work comes through the test, God will reward him on that day. The people he faithfully helped build on Christ will be like a crown of joy to him.

If his work burns up, he loses the reward he could have had. He does not lose his salvation, because salvation is God's free gift and he stayed on the true foundation. He is saved like a man who escapes a burning house with nothing left. The fire tests the work, not the worker.
Together the believers are God's temple, the holy place where God lives. God lives among them by his Holy Spirit. Later, in 6:19, Paul also says the same about each believer's body.

The same word is used twice: if anyone destroys God's temple, God will destroy him. This warns people who wreck the church through false teaching or splits. They are different from the weak builders of verse 15, who are still saved. The church is holy, so God takes how we treat it seriously.

Paul warns them not to fool themselves. Anyone who thinks he is wise by the world's standards should be willing to look foolish to the world. That means trusting God's teaching instead of his own cleverness. That is how a person becomes truly wise.

What the world calls wisdom is foolish in God's eyes. Paul quotes Job 5:13 and Psalm 94:11 to prove it. God catches crafty people in their own traps. He knows that even their best thinking is empty without him.

So stop boasting about human leaders and forming groups around them. Teachers exist for the church's good, not the church for them. Saying "I follow Paul" is far too small when everything is already yours in Christ.

All God's servants belong to you, whether Paul, Apollos or Peter, along with the world, life, death, today and the future. God uses all of them for your good. Even death becomes a servant that brings you home to God. All this is yours only because you belong to Christ. Christ, as the one who brings us to God, belongs to God, and this does not make him any less divine.
